newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-KERNEN PULLS OFF SWISS UPSET.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-KERNEN PULLS OFF SWISS UPSET.

text.p: Bruno Kernen won the men's downhill and surprised himself and everybody else at the Alpine skiing world championships on Saturday.
Kernen's victory gave the Swiss their first gold in four years after a string of favourites had tried and failed to dominate the treacherous Kandahar piste.
Kernen, starting 14th and after the three men who have dominated the downhill scene this season, clocked one minute 51.11 seconds after a near-faultless run.
Norway's Lasse Kjus was second in 1:51.18 while Italy's Kristian Ghedina, a favourite, was third in 1:51.46 just 0.01 ahead of Austrian frontrunner Fritz Strobl.
Ironically, the last Swiss to win a world title was downhiller Urs Lehmann in the 1993 championships -- another surprise that went against previous form.

The 24-year-old Swiss, who crashed badly at Wengen last month and almost retired in 1996 to pursue a career in roller-hockey, has long been touted at home as a successor to the great Pirmin Zurbriggen but has had a poor season.
He won a surprising silver medal in the combined event on Thursday, which restored a lot of his confidence. "I just tried to stay calm and I managed it," he said.
He admitted to hidden hopes, saying that "I was my own secret favourite", but he was still shocked.
"I thought I would be in the top five but I never thought I could win," he said celebrating his gold medal.
Nor had any of the other top racers.
"I thought I'd be on the podium," confessed a bitterly-disappointed Fritz Strobl. "I never thought I'd see Kernen and Kjus up there ahead of me."
The Austrian had been more than one second faster than Ghedina at one intermediate timing but lost it when he slipped on a treacherous curve on the lower part of the piste.
Ghedina, whose fans had already started celebrating his victory before Kernen and Kjus put paid to it, said Kernen had done nothing in training to suggest he was a danger.
"A gold medal in Italy would have been the most," he said ruefully. "I feel a bit like Hubert Strolz."
Austrian Strolz, now retired, had a reputation for missing the big one as "Mr Second Place" throughout his career despite taking gold in the 1988 Olympics in Calgary.
In many ways, the icy piste helped the outsiders.
The much-fancied Austrians Werner Franz and Josef Strobl both went out before Kernen entered the start house.
Franz careered heavily into the side-netting and later walked away clutching his left arm and wrist.
French World Cup champion Luc Alphand suffered the most spectacular and eye-watering crash, his skis parting from under him on a straight run and forcing him into the splits.
Alphand, bronze medallist last year and France's big hope for a first downhill gold since 1968, appeared unhurt and said that he had made a mistake with his edges.
"It's better to fall than to have a bad result," he said.
Defending 1996 champion Patrick Ortlieb skewed sideways violently higher up but regained his balance.
Remarkably the big man finished eighth.
"It was extremely icy. The sun broke the piste up and we had cracks that weren't there in training," he said.
Before this week, Kernen's best result of the season was a third in a World Cup combined event in January.
Neither Kernen nor Kjus, who has been recovering from illness, have been on a downhill podium this season.
For both men, it was their second medal of the championships. "This is my best result in downhill in about a year," said Kjus..
"The main thing is to have a Norwegian on the podium."
